name: Liam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the Cobb Ridge iron ore pit, twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off. You start at six with the pre-start check, walk round the truck, kick the tyres that are taller than me, and then it's up and down the ramp all day, shovel to crusher, shovel to crusher. I like the quiet up in the cab and I like the other drivers on the radio. What wears me out is nights, and the way my back feels after the second one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on the trucks, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years on trucks, before that I was in a sawmill that closed. My partner Annie works in the school canteen, and our two are grown, Kerry's a dental nurse in the city and Dean fixes cars in town. We rent, and honestly there's not much in the bank, maybe two or three weeks of bills if the pay stopped. I've got about four years till I can get my pension, and I count them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it's a lot of noise from people who've never been down a pit. At the union meeting I'd say the robots were never the computers, they were always the company. I don't go on the internet much, so that'd be the pub and the crib room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change much for me, because the threat at Cobb Ridge was never the chatbot stuff. They've already got driverless trucks running at the sister mine two hours north, and that's going ahead whatever the hype does. So I'd still be looking over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving and keep my head down, honestly. I'd keep paying my union dues and go to the meetings about the driverless trial, because that's where the real fight is. I won't be signing up for any course on a computer, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of a knot still there. It'd be like hearing the storm turned away but the roof's still leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sister mine. What have you actually heard from there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mate of mine, Rocco, was on trucks up there. They moved him to the wash bay when the driverless ones came in, then they cut the wash bay to one shift. He went from driving a truck worth five million to hosing one down, and he still says thank you to the shift boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the money stopped tomorrow, what's the first bill that wouldn't get paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent's sacred, so it'd be the car loan on the pickup, and then the phone. Annie would keep the lights on with the canteen pay but that's about it. We'd be at Dean's for Sunday tea a lot more.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was all noise from folk who've never been down a pit. I'd say at the union meeting that the real threat was always the company, not the computer.
S0.think: Privately I know the driverless trucks at the sister mine are coming either way, so the hype dying down doesn't save my seat. I'd still be watching my back for the next four years.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps his head down. Keeps paying union dues and attends every meeting about the driverless trial, but signs up for no computer courses.
S0.feel: Relieved, but with a knot that doesn't go away, because the robot trucks were already on their way.
S0.quote: He went from driving a truck worth five million to hosing one down, and he still says thank you to the shift boss.
S0.fieldNote: Liam separates AI from robots very sharply: chatbots mean nothing to him, the driverless haul trucks two hours north mean everything. Even in the mildest picture his savings of two or three weeks keep him on edge. The story of his mate Rocco moving to the wash bay is his reference point for every later scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has to share the gains with the people who dug the hole for them. I'd be pushing the union for a deal: no forced redundancies before pension age, and retraining paid on company time. That's what I'd say at work and I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, steady change at a mine means trucks. The trucks go first because they're the easiest, they run on fixed roads. If Cobb Ridge puts in a driverless fleet in the next few years I'm the exact person who gets moved to the wash bay or shown the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be at the union office the week it starts, asking what the agreement says about automation, and I'd want my name on any list for redeployment. I'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and stop the satellite TV, that's about eighty a month. And I'd ask Kerry to help me read whatever papers they hand out, because I'm no good with the computer forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, if I'm honest. Four years is not long, but it's long enough for them to get me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be redeployed. What job at the mine would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything that keeps me to pension age, wash bay, tyre shop, flagging on the road crew. I'm not proud. I'd rather sweep the crib room for four years than sit at home waiting for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if Cobb Ridge went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The board and the shareholders in the city, who've never set foot on the ramp. And the government, for letting them write off the robots against tax while the town loses its wages. Not the young engineers, they're just doing what they're paid to do.

S1.say: I'd say the company has to share the gains with the people who did the digging. I'd push the union hard for no forced redundancies before pension age and retraining on company time.
S1.think: Off the record, steady change at a mine means trucks first, and that's my seat. I think I'm exactly the one who'd end up in the wash bay or out the gate.
S1.do: Goes to the union office in the first week to check the automation clauses and puts his name down for redeployment. Cuts the Friday takeaway and satellite TV, about eighty a month, and asks his daughter to help with the paperwork.
S1.feel: Sick in the stomach, because four years is short but still long enough to lose the job before the pension.
S1.quote: I'd rather sweep the crib room for four years than sit at home waiting for a letter.
S1.fieldNote: This is where Liam's worry becomes concrete: haul trucks are the first thing a mine automates, and he knows it. He blames the board and the government, not the engineers, which fits his union politics. He would take any job to reach pension age, and there's no pride in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster made in boardrooms and someone has to stop it. I'd want the union out on the road with banners, and the government to put a brake on it. Online I'd leave it to Dean, he's the one with the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years I'm not even at pension age. I'd be sixty, no job, no savings, and no other pit within a day's drive that'd take a truck driver when all the trucks drive themselves. I don't know what a man my age does when the thing he's good at just disappears overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd go to the union and to the welfare office to find out what we'd get. I'd ask the pension fund if I can take it early, even with less. We'd probably give up the rental and move in with Dean and his girlfriend, that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, the kind where you lie awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have two years' warning, more or less. Does that two years help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Two years is long enough to watch it come and not long enough to get to my pension, so it's the worst of both. Maybe I'd start saving the overtime, but overtime goes first when they're cutting back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Annie the night you knew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll be all right, because that's what you say. Then I'd go out to the shed and sit there for an hour. She'd know anyway, she always does.

S2.say: I'd call it a disaster made in boardrooms and say someone has to stop it. I'd want the union on the road with banners and the government putting a brake on it.
S2.think: Privately, two years leaves me at sixty with no job, no savings and no other pit nearby that would want a truck driver. I don't know what someone my age does when the one thing he's good at disappears.
S2.do: Goes to the union and the welfare office in the first month to see what support exists. Asks the pension fund about taking it early on reduced terms, and plans to give up the rental and move in with his son.
S2.feel: Properly scared, lying awake doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: I don't know what a man my age does when the thing he's good at just disappears overnight.
S2.fieldNote: Two years lands Liam in the gap between job and pension with almost nothing saved, and he sees no way to close it. He reaches for public support and family straight away, which fits his politics and his means. The moment he'd tell Annie 'we'll be all right' and then sit in the shed was the most honest part of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say the union needs to get in early this time and lock down a deal. Five years is enough time for a proper fight, not just a protest. I'd say that in the crib room every day till people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is right on the edge for me. I'd be sixty-three, and that's close enough to the pension that a decent payout could carry us across. So for me it's all about whether the company plays fair at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the pickup payments by selling it and buying something old for cash, that frees up about three hundred a month to put away. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a bridging payment to pension age for anyone over fifty-five. I'd stay on the trucks as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a different anxious. With two years I'm drowning, with five I can see the far bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between a pension and the welfare office. Three years of saving three hundred is about ten thousand, which isn't much but it's more than I've ever had. And three more years of pension contributions going in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd never do a computer course. With five years, would you reconsider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if it was the union running it and it was something practical, like being one of the people who looks after the robot trucks when they break. But I'd be fooling myself. I'm fifty-eight and I still ring Kerry to send a photo on my phone.

S3.say: I'd say the union has to get in early and lock down a deal this time, because five years is long enough for a real fight. I'd keep saying it in the crib room until people were sick of hearing it.
S3.think: Off the record, five years puts me at sixty-three, close enough that a fair payout could carry us to the pension. It all comes down to whether the company plays fair at the end.
S3.do: Sells the pickup and buys an old car for cash, saving about three hundred a month. Pushes the union for a bridging payment to pension age for workers over fifty-five, and stays on the trucks as long as he can.
S3.feel: Still anxious, but now he can see an end to it rather than drowning.
S3.quote: I'm fifty-eight and I still ring Kerry to send a photo on my phone.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter hugely to Liam because they almost reach his pension. He found a real lever, selling the pickup, but admitted he wouldn't retrain even with time. His joke about ringing his daughter to send a photo was half a joke and half a confession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse for anyone getting dumped. Train the young ones for whatever comes next and look after the old ones. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, in ten years I'm sixty-eight and long gone from the pit, if my back lasts. So it's not my job I'd worry about, it's Dean, and the town. Every shop on Station Road lives off mine wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd do anyway, keep driving and get to my pension. I'd tell Dean to get his electrical ticket, because someone has to fix the robots. And I'd still be at the union meetings, because the young ones need someone who remembers the sawmill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's like watching weather coming over the hills when you're nearly home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sawmill. What happened there that you'd want the young ones to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They closed it with six weeks' notice and everyone said there'll be other jobs. There weren't, not in town, half the men ended up driving to the coast. Ten years' warning is nothing if nobody uses it, and nobody used it at the sawmill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to the town by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. If the mine runs itself it doesn't need the houses or the pub or the football club. Maybe it pays a bit of tax to keep things going, but I wouldn't bet on it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly, so nobody should get dumped. Train the young ones for what comes next and look after the older ones.
S4.think: Privately, by 2036 I'm sixty-eight and gone from the pit, so it's not my own job I'd worry about. I'd worry about my son and about a town where every shop lives off mine wages.
S4.do: Keeps driving until his pension at about sixty-two. Urges his son to get an electrical ticket so he can work on the machines, and keeps going to union meetings to pass on what happened at the sawmill.
S4.feel: More uneasy than scared, like weather coming over the hills when he's nearly home.
S4.quote: Ten years' warning is nothing if nobody uses it, and nobody used it at the sawmill.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Liam's own job mostly clears his pension date, so his worry shifts to his son and the town. He still doesn't fully relax, because his thin savings and the sawmill closure taught him that warning rarely turns into help. The lesson he would pass on is about time being wasted, not about technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because it lands right in the gap before my pension. What would help is a bridge, a payment from the company or the government that carries anyone over fifty-five to pension age. I don't want a handout for ever, just to get across. I've paid my dues for twenty-two years, I just want to be standing when I get to the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my back. Everyone talks about robots taking the jobs, but the truck already half took my back. If a robot drove nights and I drove days, I'd be happy, but nobody ever offers that.

headlineQuote: I've paid my dues for twenty-two years, I just want to be standing when I get to the end.
portrait: Liam Moreau is 58 and has driven haul trucks at the Cobb Ridge iron ore pit for twenty-two years, after a sawmill he worked at closed with six weeks' notice. He rents, has two or three weeks of savings and counts the four years to his pension. A strong union man, he never uses AI tools and sees the driverless trucks at the company's sister mine as the real threat in every picture. He swings from uneasy in the hype scenario to panicked when AGI comes in two years, and he calms only when ten years would carry him past his pension date. What he wants is a bridge to retirement, not a new career.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would end his job before he reaches his pension, with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A bridging payment from the company or the government that carries workers over fifty-five to pension age.
